extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of English poetry; poets and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for recognizing, composing, and judging poetry (what makes language poetic, suitable subjects, and effective poetic devices), drawn from literary-criticism lectures on English poets. Emphasis on imagination, passion, musicality, and appropriateness of subject and form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination / heightening beyond mere description
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere description of natural objects, nor a mere delineation of natural feelings ... constitutes the ultimate end and aim of poetry, without the heightenings of the imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry must heighten ordinary impressions via the imagination rather than merely reporting facts or feelings; critics who reduce poetry to literal truth misunderstand its purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestiveness / evocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry represents forms chiefly as they suggest other forms; feelings, as they suggest forms or other feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective poetry evokes associations and resonances beyond the immediate object — it 'suggests what exists out of it' rather than merely depicting the object itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Movement and dynamism (describing the flowing, not the fixed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry puts a spirit of life and motion into the universe. It describes the flowing, not the fixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should convey progress, suspense, and the inner motion of events (the interval of expectation) rather than static tableaux; this is part of its imaginative power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intensity / overflowing poetic impression
rubrics_metrics.description: The poetical impression of any object is that uneasy, exquisite sense of beauty or power that cannot be contained within itself; that is impatient of all limit ... strives to link itself to some other image of kindred beauty or grandeur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affective intensity that seeks expansion or linkage to other images is a mark of poetry; the impression should feel excessive and generative rather than contained and ordinary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective truth: fidelity to impression under passion
rubrics_metrics.description: This language is not the less true to nature, because it is false in point of fact; but so much the more true and natural, if it conveys the impression which the object under the influence of passion makes on the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic truth is judged by psychological/verbal fidelity to felt impression under passion, not by literal factual accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginative transformation / permissible distortion
rubrics_metrics.description: Let an object ... be presented to the senses in a state of agitation or fear — and the imagination will distort or magnify the object, and convert it into the likeness of whatever is most proper to encourage the fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distortion, exaggeration, or personification that serves feeling (e.g., 'each bush suppos'd a bear') is legitimate poetic device; poets may reshape perception to express inner states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of comparison, contrast, and climax (especially in tragic poetry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic poetry ... strives to carry on the feeling to the utmost point of sublimity or pathos, by all the force of comparison or contrast; loses the sense of present suffering in the imaginary exaggeration of it; exhausts the terror or pity by an unlimited indulgence of it ... brings every moment ... in startling review before us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In tragedy, comparative and contrasting images, escalation, and imaginative exaggeration are tools to intensify pathos or sublimity; the dramatic shaping of passion (climax, whirl of events) is crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to whole human constitution (moral, intellectual, and sensitive faculties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Impassioned poetry is an emanation of the moral and intellectual part of our nature, as well as of the sensitive ... and ought to appeal to these different parts of our constitution, in order to be perfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great poetry engages feeling, will, and understanding; works that appeal almost exclusively to sensibility (domestic/prose tragedy) are less fully poetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of image, words, and feeling (the perfect coincidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the perfect coincidence of the image and the words with the feeling we have ... that gives an instant 'satisfaction to the thought.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry succeeds when diction and imagery are naturally fused with the felt emotion, giving immediate aesthetic satisfaction; mismatch undermines poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musicality, rhythm, and sustained harmony (including appropriate use of rhyme and blank verse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry combines the ordinary use of language with musical expression ... the musical in sound is the sustained and continuous; the musical in thought is the sustained and continuous also. Rhyme is but fair ... rhyme assists the memory; may not it also quicken the fancy?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic rhythm and musical arrangement of syllables are essential to poetry's effect; rhyme can aid memory and fancy but can become tiresome if excessively sweet or uniform (Pope criticized), while blank verse can be ideal for dramatic dialogue (Shakespeare praised).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate subject matter: novelty, the undefined, and non-didactic topics
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the undefined and uncommon that gives birth and scope to the imagination; we can only fancy what we do not know. Nothing is a subject for poetry that admits of a dispute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose subjects that allow imaginative enlargement (the novel, mysterious, or visionary) rather than didactic, argumentative, or dryly abstract topics; poetry aims at instantaneous sympathy, not persuasive disputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestive capacity versus concreteness (poetry implies beyond the literal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Painting gives the object itself; poetry what it implies. Painting embodies what a thing contains in itself: poetry suggests what exists out of it ... as it relates to passion, painting gives the event, poetry the progress of events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer implication and evocation over literal completeness; poetry should open outward associations and temporal development rather than present a finished picture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to elevate and fix the imagination ('married to immortal verse')
rubrics_metrics.description: That which lifts the spirit above the earth, which draws the soul out of itself with indescribable longings, is poetry in kind, and generally fit to become so in name, by being 'married to immortal verse.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works that permanently fix the imagination and elevate the spirit (examples: Pilgrim's Progress, Robinson Crusoe's reflective passages) approach poetic status; the power to 'fix' a reader's imagination is a mark of poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of forced sympathy and mechanical artifice (authentic spontaneity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The interest is worked up to an inconceivable height ... by an infinite number of little things, by incessant labour ... The sympathy excited is not a voluntary contribution, but a tax. Nothing is unforced and spontaneous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should arise from spontaneous imaginative impulse rather than contrived, mechanical accumulation of effects (criticism of Richardson); artifice that drags the fancy rather than lets it run ahead is an anti-pattern.
